rv.q: But I don't think the uneven show really worked on opening night, for several reasons.
It results in a show as deliriously entertaining as it is astonishingly profound.
McPherson’s script is surprisingly and pleasingly funny.
Go see this play. Folks will be talking about it long after it closes.
McPherson has deftly heightened the impact of the core of Strindberg’s work, finding the key to the characters and dynamics much of which honestly I could not see in the original.
In the knowing minds of both Mr. Strindberg and Mr. McPherson, we are held in total thrall by an excellent cast and crew that step so boldly toward such storytelling.
THE DANCE OF DEATH is exceptionally well done. It perfectly illustrates unhappily ever after and makes us laugh at it.

Now being mounted in a handsome new production at Steppenwolf, I suspect your opinion of this lively new-ish adaptation by Conor McPherson of one of the classics of the theatrical canon will depend on whether you view the source material as a drama with comic elements, or a scabrous black comedy.
Full of physical and verbal tics and abrupt tonal shifts that somehow add up to a fully realized character, it's a performance worth seeing.
And “The Dance of Death” certainly offers loads of dark humor and devious drama for everyone to sink their teeth into.
Like an expressionist painting, it exaggerates and distorts for effect.

Although I applaud director Yasen Peyankov's work on The Dance of Death and his use of an ensemble cast and engaging humor, the production needs more of Strindberg's grit and bleakness to balance the humor.
This production is one that you should truly make it a point to witness.
This is a fascinating comedy with both broad and sophisticated humor, beautifully staged.
The set design is awesome but the dialog seems stilted, it’s a bit long, and the play overall is just not as satisfying as I had hoped.
The length and density of the exchanges dilute moments of tension, preventing the drama from fully sustaining its emotional impact.

cn.t: McPherson's adaptation of Strindberg's toxic marriage drama finds surprisingly dark comedy at Steppenwolf, with critics praising Perry and Erbe's performances and Pollard's stunning set, though some find the bleak material more unsettling than funny.
